q7.answer: Clients do not hold the key. On each outbound call they ask SecretCache for the current key and build the Authorization header. The 5-minute refresh atomically swaps the cached entry, so the next call uses the new key, and in-flight requests finish with the old one.

q8.answer: In B8, platform checks that every pod runs the new image and the pod list matches the current pod count. Each pod's cluster-internal version endpoint must report exactly the B3 version ids for all three keys. Any other consumer found in B1 must have been moved, and the provider's 'last used' for the old key should show no recent use. Any mismatch means no revoke. Security on-call also approves before revoking.

q9.answer: Order: B1 check providers and consumers; B2 set store access (paths, KMS, policies); B3 rotate at the providers (new key created, old left active) and write the new keys into the store, with a validation job; B4/B5 code PR (switch the app to the store, remove keys from app.yaml, add the CI guard) merged and built; B6/B7 rolling deploy; B8 confirm; B9 revoke old keys. The old keys are never copied into the store. The store receives only new keys, and removal from the file happens in the same PR as the switch to reading from the store.

q10.answer: A local run (`make run`, which sets APP_ENV=local) reads orders-api/dev/* from the dev store using the developer's own identity. Those paths hold sandbox or test keys, never live ones. Providers with no sandbox use a local fake client. Developers have no access to prod paths.

q11.answer: I never decided this explicitly. By implication, A1 requires all three to load and be non-empty, so a missing secret is treated as a failure: retry 3 times 2 seconds apart, then exit non-zero without becoming ready. However, I did not specify whether a not-found error (as opposed to an unreachable store) is retried or fails immediately, and the plan does not say so.
